extracted.intended_audience: NLP / ML researchers and practitioners working on headline generation, summarization, and reinforcement learning (especially for news/headline tasks)
extracted.subtask_description: Generating sensational (attention-grabbing) news headlines from input articles without human-labeled sensationalism data, using a learned sensationalism scorer and reinforcement learning with a dynamic MLE/RL balance (Auto-tuned Reinforcement Learning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture attention / generate reader interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A good headline needs to capture people’s attention and serve as an irresistible invitation for users to read through the article (e.g., “$2 Billion Worth of Free Media for Trump” is considered better than a pure summarization-style headline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headlines differ from summaries: they do not need to contain most important information but should entice clicks/reads. Evaluation of headline methods should consider this attention/engagement objective in addition to content relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism score (αsen) — learned sensationalism scorer
rubrics_metrics.description: Train a sensationalism scorer that outputs an intensity score αsen for a headline (used to measure how sensational a headline is and used as an RL reward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scorer is trained by classifying 'sensational' headlines (many comments) against 'non-sensational' baseline headlines generated from a summarization model. The learned αsen is noisy/fragile and can be fooled; this must be accounted for in downstream optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distant supervision for sensationalism dataset construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect positive samples as headlines receiving many comments from popular online websites and negative samples as headlines generated by a summarization model (pointer-generator baseline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: human-annotated clickbait datasets are small/expensive; using many-comment headlines cheaply captures a variety of sensationalization patterns. Using generated-baseline negatives leverages style-obfuscation properties of summarization/back-translation. An alternative (few-comments negatives) was tried but generalized worse in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism scorer training architecture & settings
rubrics_metrics.description: One-layer CNN for binary classification trained with binary cross-entropy loss Lsen to predict αsen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical settings: 1-D convolution filter sizes {1,3,5}; embedding size 300 (initialized from Qiu et al. trained on Weibo, fixed during training); Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.0001. Dataset sizes reported (e.g., 170,754 training positive, balanced negative samples). Reported scorer performance: 0.65 accuracy and 0.65 avg F1 on test set (vs 0.50 random).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensationalism score as RL reward (Rsen = αsen(ys))
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the predicted sensationalism score of a sampled generated headline ys as the reinforcement learning reward to encourage more sensational outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because αsen is learned and noisy it can be exploited by RL to produce unnatural phrases that nonetheless get high αsen (example where an unnatural sentence scored 0.99996). Treating αsen directly as reward requires mechanisms to prevent reward hacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auto-tuned Reinforcement Learning (ARL) — dynamic MLE/RL balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss LARL-SEN = (1 − αsen(y*)) LRL + αsen(y*) LMLE, i.e., dynamically weight RL vs MLE per training sample using the sensationalism score of the reference headline y*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If αsen(y*) is high (training headline is sensational), favor MLE to imitate that sample; if low, favor RL to increase sensationalism. This sample-dependent weighting mitigates the conflict between inconsistent objectives of MLE (fluency/reconstruction) and RL (maximize reward), and reduces tendency to generate unnatural phrases when the reward is noisy.

rubrics_metrics.name: MLE objective for fluency and readability (LMLE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum likelihood estimation training minimizes the negative log-likelihood of training headlines (LMLE = −(1/T) ∑ log P(y*_t)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MLE acts as a language model to maintain readability/fluency; combining MLE with RL is necessary to avoid RL-only degenerate/ungrammatical outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinforcement learning training details — REINFORCE and baseline for variance reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the REINFORCE algorithm: sample ys from generator, compute reward R (ROUGE or αsen), and optimize LRL = −(1/T) ∑ (R − Ř_t) log P(w_t) where Ř_t is a learned baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baseline reward Ř_t is estimated by a linear model Ř_t = W_r o_t + b_r trained by minimizing mean squared error between R and Ř_t (Lb = (1/T) ∑ |R − Ř_t|^2). Sampling-based training and baseline regression are required to reduce variance of policy gradients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naive fixed-mix of RL and MLE (λ-mix) as baseline and λ tuning
rubrics_metrics.description: A common baseline mixes RL and MLE via LRL-* = λ LRL + (1 − λ) LMLE with a fixed λ across samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior work used very large λ (e.g., 0.9984). In practice λ should be tuned by validation metric (e.g., ROUGE-L). The paper used λ=0.95 for Pointer-Gen+RL-ROUGE; for Pointer-Gen+RL-SEN they used λ=0.5 (with min sensationalism filtering) to avoid unnatural phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter training samples by minimum αsen to avoid RL domination
rubrics_metrics.description: When training ARL/ARL-SEN, filter out training headlines with a sensationalism score ≤ 0.1 (use only headlines with αsen > 0.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the predicted αsen distribution is heavily concentrated near 0, which would cause, on average, RL to dominate (e.g., expectation yields 0.239 MLE and 0.761 RL per sample) and produce unnatural outputs. Filtering low-αsen samples reduces RL dominance and improves stability and fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation — ROUGE metrics for relevance (RG-1, RG-2, RG-L)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and ROUGE-L (pyrouge toolkit) to measure n-gram overlap between generated and reference headlines to evaluate relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ROUGE assesses relevance/summarization quality; ARL-optimized models should retain reasonable ROUGE to ensure they still summarize the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human evaluation: binary sensationalism and fluency annotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Human evaluation uses two independent annotation tasks: 'Is the headline sensational?' and 'Is the headline fluent?'; each headline is labeled by 10 annotators blind to system source via CrowdFlower. Sensationalism/fluency scores are defined as proportion of 'yes' annotations across all headlines from a model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple annotators per item and blind allocation. Report proportions and assess statistical significance across systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance testing for sensationalism improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare sensationalism scores across models using Chi-square tests (report p-values to support claims of improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports that Pointer-Gen+ARL-SEN is statistically significantly more sensational than comparators (largest p-value < 0.01) and that RL-based models outperform ROUGE-only models with p < 0.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model architecture requirement: Pointer-Generator with copy mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a Pointer-Generator (Pointer-Gen) network to generate headlines, enabling copying of rare/unknown words from the input article via a p_gen mixture between vocabulary distribution and attention-based copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The copy mechanism helps preserve factual/rare tokens (e.g., names, numbers) which is important for news headline generation. Implement attention (Luong-style) and pointer gating as in See et al. (2017).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset & preprocessing recommendations (LCSTS, Tencent News; tokenization/vocab)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use LCSTS for headline generation training (2.4M training samples, 10,666 validation, 725 test); use Tencent News headlines as positive sensational samples. Tokenize with Jieba and use a vocab size of ~50,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide train/val/test splits, fix embeddings where beneficial, and be mindful of dataset distribution differences when sampling positives/negatives for the sensationalism scorer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain summarization relevance while optimizing sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when optimizing for sensationalism, the model should retain summarization ability (Pointer-Gen+ARL-SEN achieves comparable ROUGE scores to Pointer-Gen baseline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor ROUGE alongside sensationalism and fluency to ensure the model does not drift away from content relevance while increasing sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed sensationalization strategies (desirable tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective sensationalization strategies include creating a curiosity gap, asking questions, highlighting numbers, using emotional words, and empathizing with the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in Table 4 illustrate tactics the model learned (e.g., asking 'Will India become the next China?', emphasizing numbers like '500 billion', emotional exaggeration). These are acceptable/expected forms of sensationalization but should be balanced against factuality and fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical consideration: potential harms of generating sensational headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Generating sensational headlines raises ethical questions about intentionally producing attention-grabbing (possibly exaggerated or misleading) news headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Future work should investigate ethics, improve the sensationalism scorer to avoid harmful manipulations, and consider safeguards when deploying sensational headline generators in real-world journalism contexts.
